library(tidyverse)

# Reading in Data

```{r}
# Here latin1 encoding fixes the invalid string errors caused by the degree variables
bike <- read_csv("https://www4.stat.ncsu.edu/~online/datasets/SeoulBikeData.csv", 
                 locale = locale(encoding = "latin1")
)
bike
```

# EDA

## Checking Data

### 1. Missingness

```{r}
colSums(is.na(bike))
```
No columns have missing values, so we dont need to drop anything


### 2. Column types and values

```{r}
glimpse(bike)
```
Here date is read in as a character variable, and seasons, holiday, and functioning day should be factors.

Summary stats for numeric columns

```{r}
bike |>
  select(where(is.numeric)) |>
  summary()
```
These ranges look normal. Humidity has a minimum of 0, which shouldn't happen outside. This may be a sensor problem, but we'll leave it in

Unique values for categorical variables:

```{r}
bike |>
  select(where(is.character), -Date) |>
  map(unique)
```
Here are the unique values for categorical variables that will have to be turned into factors, their counts are below

```{r}
bike |>
  count(Seasons)

bike |>
  count(Holiday)

bike |>
  count(`Functioning Day`)
```

### 3. Convert date

```{r}
bike <- bike |>
  mutate(Date = dmy(Date))
# Checking for anything that failed to parse
sum(is.na(bike$Date))
```
```{r}
range(bike$Date)
```

### 4. Convert to factors

```{r}
bike <- bike |>
  mutate(across(c(Seasons, Holiday, `Functioning Day`), as.factor))

bike
```

### 5. Rename variables 

```{r}
# Using lower snake case here
bike_data <- bike |>
  rename(
    date = Date,
    bike_count = `Rented Bike Count`,
    hour = Hour,
    temp = starts_with("Temperature"),
    humidity = `Humidity(%)`,
    wind_speed = `Wind speed (m/s)`,
    visibility = `Visibility (10m)`,
    dew_point_temp = starts_with("Dew point"),
    solar_radiation = `Solar Radiation (MJ/m2)`,
    rainfall = `Rainfall(mm)`,
    snowfall = `Snowfall (cm)`,
    seasons = Seasons,
    holiday = Holiday,
    functioning_day = `Functioning Day`
  )

names(bike_data)
```

### 6. Summary stats

```{r}
# Function to summarize by given grouping variables
bike_summary <- function(data, ...) {
  data |>
    group_by(...) |>
    summarize(
      n = n(),
      total = sum(bike_count),
      mean = mean(bike_count),
      sd = sd(bike_count),
      min = min(bike_count),
      median = median(bike_count),
      max = max(bike_count),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
}

bike_data |> bike_summary()
```

```{r}
bike_data |> bike_summary(seasons)
```

```{r}
bike_data |> bike_summary(holiday)
```

```{r}
bike_data |> bike_summary(functioning_day)
```

When functioning_day is zero, the bike rental total is 0 since no bikes are rented if the system isn't functioning. We can drop these to only focus on functioning hours

```{r}
bike_data <- bike_data |>
  filter(functioning_day == "Yes") |>
  select(-functioning_day)

nrow(bike_data)
```

### 7. Summarize across hours

Here we are collapsing the hours into days

```{r}
bike_daily <- bike_data |>
  group_by(date, seasons, holiday) |>
  summarize(
    across(c(bike_count, rainfall, snowfall), sum),
    across(c(temp, humidity, wind_speed, visibility, dew_point_temp, solar_radiation), mean),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

bike_daily
```

We now have 353 rows, one for each day the system was running

### 8. Summaries from daily data

```{r}
bike_daily |> 
  select(where(is.numeric)) |>
  summary()
```


```{r}
bike_daily |> bike_summary(seasons)
```

```{r}
bike_daily |> bike_summary(holiday)
```



```{r}
bike_daily |> bike_summary(seasons, holiday)
```
The mean rentals per day is about 17,500, ranging from 977 to 36,149. Season makes a large difference, with winter averaging around 5,400 rentals. 

Holidays also average about 5,000 fewer rentals, although there is a low sample size, and most holidays occur during winter.

Correlations:

```{r}
bike_daily |>
  select(where(is.numeric)) |>
  cor() |>
  round(2)
```
Temperature (0.75) and solar radiation (0.74) have the strongest linear relationship with rentals, followed by dew point (0.65). 

Temperature and dew point are also highly correlated (0.96), so they carry very similar information.

Plots: 

Plot of daily bike rentals over the year:

```{r}
season_colors <- c(
  Winter = "lightblue",
  Spring = "springgreen",
  Summer = "orange",
  Autumn = "yellow"
)


ggplot(bike_daily, aes(date, bike_count, color = seasons)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = 1), linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = season_colors) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 months", date_labels = "%b %Y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Bikes rented per day", color = "Season")
```
Rentals stay low through winter, climb through spring, Peak in June and again around September.

Bike rentals by season and holiday

```{r}
ggplot(bike_daily, aes(seasons, bike_count, color = seasons)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ holiday) +
  scale_color_manual(values = season_colors, guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Bikes rented per day")

```
The holiday boxplots are misleading because of the lack of data, but non-holidays show that winter has the lowest median rental amount of the four seasons. Spring has the second lowest median, but the largest spread.

Daily bike rentals with temperature

```{r}
ggplot(bike_daily, aes(temp, bike_count)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = seasons), alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, color = "black") +
  scale_color_manual(values = season_colors) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(
    title = "Daily Bike Rentals vs. Temperature",
    x = "Mean Temperature (°C)", y = "Bikes Rented per day")
```
Temperature has a clear relationship with bike rentals, but its not purely linear. Rentals fall off for the hot days, hinting at the usefulness of a squared term in our model fit.

Bike rentals with Solar radiation 

```{r}
ggplot(bike_daily, aes(solar_radiation, bike_count)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "orange") +
  labs(
    title = "Daily Bike Rentals vs. Solar Radiation",
    x = "Solar Radiation (MJ/m^2)", y = "Bikes Rented per day")
```

Bike rentals and solar radiation have a strong correlation (0.74), although sunny days tend to also be warm days,
so some of this correlation may also be explained by the temperature effect.

# Split the Data

Here we use a 75/25 split stratified on seasons
```{r}
set.seed(44)

bike_split <- rsample::initial_split(bike_daily, prop = 0.75, strata = "seasons")
bike_train <- training(bike_split)
bike_test <- testing(bike_split)
```

# Fitting MLR Models

## Preparing the data

First, we need to prepare the data by creating a day_type factor with Sunday as day 1 and
Saturday as day 7. Then, we need to standardize each numeric weather variable using our training data as a reference.
```{r}
weather_vars <- c(
  "temp", "humidity", "wind_speed", "visibility",
  "dew_point_temp", "solar_radiation", "rainfall", "snowfall"
)

standardize <- function(data, reference) {
  data |>
    mutate(
      day_type = if_else(wday(date, week_start = 7) %in% c(1, 7), "weekend", "weekday"),
      day_type = factor(day_type, levels = c("weekday", "weekend")),
      across(
        all_of(weather_vars),
        \(x) (x - mean(reference[[cur_column()]])) / sd(reference[[cur_column()]]),
        .names = "{.col}_std"
      )
    )
}
```

```{r}
train_std <- standardize(bike_train, reference = bike_train)
test_std <- standardize(bike_test, reference = bike_train)
```

Checking standardization results, training variables should have a mean of approximately 0 and standard
deviation of 1. Test set should be close but not exact.

```{r}
bind_rows(train = train_std, test = test_std, .id = "set") |>
  group_by(set) |>
  summarize(
    temp_std_mean = mean(temp_std),
    temp_std_sd = sd(temp_std),
    rainfall_std_mean = mean(rainfall_std),
    rainfall_std_sd = sd(rainfall_std)
  )
```

## Fitting models

### Model 1: Main effects

```{r}
formula_1 <- bike_count ~ temp_std + humidity_std + wind_speed_std + visibility_std +
  dew_point_temp_std + solar_radiation_std + rainfall_std + snowfall_std +
  seasons + holiday + day_type
```

### Model 2: Interactions

```{r}
formula_2 <- update(
  formula_1,
  . ~ . + seasons:holiday + seasons:temp_std + temp_std:rainfall_std
)
```

### Model 3: Quadratic terms

```{r}
formula_3 <- update(
  formula_2,
  . ~ . + I(temp_std^2) + I(humidity_std^2)
)
```

```{r}
model_formulas <- list(
  "Model 1" = formula_1,
  "Model 2" = formula_2,
  "Model 3" = formula_3
)

model_fits <- map(model_formulas, \(f) lm(f, data = train_std))
```

## Comparing test set RMSE

```{r}
rmse <- function(actual, predicted) {
  sqrt(mean((actual - predicted)^2))
}

test_rmse <- map_dbl(
  model_fits,
  \(fit) rmse(test_std$bike_count, predict(fit, newdata = test_std))
)
```

```{r}
tibble(model = names(test_rmse), test_rmse = test_rmse)

best_model <- names(which.min(test_rmse))
```

Our best model has the lowest test set RMSE, so we select Model 3. Although Model 2 is also a good choice, adding the interaction
terms appear to do a lot of heavy lifting.

## Fitting best model to full dataset

```{r}
bike_full_std <- standardize(bike_daily, reference = bike_daily)

final_fit <- lm(model_formulas[[best_model]], data = bike_full_std)

coef(summary(final_fit)) |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "term") |>
  select(term, estimate = Estimate, std_error = `Std. Error`, t_value = `t value`)
```

Here is the final model fit. Is has an intercept of 18061, which is the prediction for a baseline day with 
all weather variables constant. Rentals increase as temperature and solar radiation increase, whereas rentals decrease as humidity and wind speed increase.  

```{r}
summary(final_fit)$adj.r.squared
```

The final model has an adjusted R-squared of 0.917, although this is measured on the same data used to fit the model, so the test
RMSE is a better guide of prediction.
